particle indicating potentiality

a potential particle, about whose force and meaning Apollonius in On Syntax 3, 6 p. 205, 3 correctly and clearly teaches: “the conjunction wishes to do away with the actual occurrence of events, turning them into possibility, whence it is also called ‘potential’. For ‘I wrote’ or ‘I was writing’ or ‘I had written’ are either partially completed or completed long ago; therefore it attaches to those capable of receiving its material: ‘I would be writing’, ‘I would have written’, ‘I would have written’; but not to ‘I write’ or ‘I will write’; for it is not past, so that the conjunction’s removal of the actual occurrence and promise of the future may be possible.” A much fuller explanation, but not free from errors, is that of the grammarian in Bekker’s Anecdota p. 126-128. This particle is always attached to a verb, either expressed or understood from the preceding. Regarding the tenses and moods of verbs with which it can be constructed, the following must be noted:
It is constructed with the imperfect or aorist in the apodosis after a conditional clause.
With no preceding conditional clause
[Faulty at line 1252: ἡ κάρτ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἂν παρεσκόπεις χρησμῶν ἐμῶν [you would have been quite overlooking my oracles], where ἄν [would] has no place.]

Regarding the optative, it must be noted that ἄν is never joined with it where it is truly a wish; and expressions that have roughly the force of wishing, πῶς ἄν [how would] and τίς ἄν [who would], when joined with the optative, are those of someone asking, not wishing; for examples see under πῶς and τίς. Not rarely ἄν is joined with the optative with the force of an imperative.
